Breaking: A little-known protein could be a powerful weapon against Alzheimer’s

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1396 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A protein that helps protect the brain may offer scientists a promising newly introduced way to fight Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia.
  • The findings, published in Science Advances by scientists at Sanford Burnham Prebys, suggest that strengthening the brain's own protective mechanisms could eventually lead to fresh treatments for neurodegenerative diseases.
  • The discovery is particularly significant because tau plays an essential role in keeping healthy brain cells functioning.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A protein that helps protect the brain may offer scientists a promising newly introduced way to fight Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia. Researchers have discovered that increasing levels of this protein can reduce the buildup of toxic tangles associated with brain damage, while also helping preserve the connections that allow nerve cells to communicate.

The findings, published in Science Advances by scientists at Sanford Burnham Prebys, suggest that strengthening the brain's own protective mechanisms could eventually lead to fresh treatments for neurodegenerative diseases. In experiments with mice, the researchers found that boosting the protein reduced several damaging changes associated with Alzheimer's, including brain shrinkage and the accumulation of abnormal tau proteins.

The discovery is particularly significant because tau plays an essential role in keeping healthy brain cells functioning. Under normal conditions, tau proteins help stabilize microtubules, tiny structures that provide internal support to neurons and help maintain the intricate networks of the nervous system.

In Alzheimer's and several related disorders, however, tau proteins can become abnormal and stick together, forming harmful clumps known as tau tangles. These tangles disrupt the normal functioning of nerve cells and are associated with cognitive decline and neuronal death. Diseases characterized by abnormal tau accumulation are collectively called tauopathies.

A Protective Protein With a Surprising Role in Alzheimer's.

The researchers investigated a protein called sorting-related receptor with A-type repeats (SORLA), which has already attracted scientific attention for its potential role in protecting the brain against Alzheimer's disease.

Previous studies have shown that SORLA can help limit the production and accumulation of amyloid-beta, another protein closely associated with Alzheimer's. Amyloid-beta can build up into plaques in the brain, making it one of the disease's major pathological hallmarks alongside tau tangles.

"In the last 15 or 20 years, considerable data has come out from our lab and other groups showing that SORLA can suppress one of the hallmarks of Alzheimer's disease -- amyloid-beta generation and accumulation," mentioned Timothy Huang, PhD, assistant professor in the Center for Neurologic Diseases at Sanford Burnham Prebys.

"Very little was known, however, about whether SORLA affected the tau tangles reflected on the other side of the coin in Alzheimer's disease.".

In a recent development, to investigate this question, the scientists developed a mouse model by breeding animals engineered to produce additional human SORLA with mice that develop tau tangles, brain atrophy, and cognitive impairments. This allowed them to examine whether higher SORLA levels could reduce tau accumulation and protect against the damage it causes.

Boosting SORLA Reduces Toxic Tau and Brain Shrinkage.

The results revealed that additional SORLA provided protection against several processes that contribute to tau tangles and the progression of neurodegenerative disease.

One key effect involved a process called hyperphosphorylation. This occurs when too many phosphate groups attach to tau proteins, altering their behavior and contributing to the development of harmful tangles. Higher SORLA levels reduced this abnormal modification.

The protein also limited the ability of misfolded tau to act as "seeds" that encourage other tau proteins to clump together. This seeding process can help toxic tau aggregates multiply and spread their damaging effects.

Beyond reducing tau abnormalities, SORLA helped preserve synapses, the specialized connections through which neurons communicate. It also protected synaptic plasticity, the brain's ability to strengthen or modify those connections, which is essential for learning, memory, and normal cognitive function.

"When you upregulate SORLA, you can suppress the negative effects found in tauopathies," mentioned Huijie Huang, PhD, a staff scientist in the Huang lab at Sanford Burnham Prebys and lead author of the study.

"We found there was less brain atrophy and less tau accumulation, which was very exciting to see.".

Removing the Protein Makes Brain Damage Worse.

After observing the benefits of increasing SORLA, the researchers examined what would happen if the protein were missing entirely.

SORLA is produced using instructions encoded by a gene called Sorl1. Some people carry mutations that interfere with this gene's function, potentially disrupting the production or activity of the protective protein.

To investigate the consequences, the team studied genetically modified mice that lacked Sorl1 and therefore could not produce SORLA.

According to recent reports, the results contrasted sharply with those seen in mice carrying additional copies of the protein. Instead of protecting against tau-related damage, the absence of SORLA made the harmful effects more severe.

"The opposite turned out to be true when we deleted the ability to produce SORLA proteins," mentioned Tim Huang, senior and corresponding author of the manuscript. "A lack of SORLA exacerbated the harmful effects observed in tauopathies.".

These contrasting results provided further evidence that SORLA plays an important protective role in the brain and may influence how severely tau-related diseases progress.

A New Clue Could Lead to Alzheimer's Treatments.

To understand why changing SORLA levels had such different effects, the researchers examined the molecular activity of individual brain cells and the surrounding tissue.

In a recent development, they combined advanced sequencing methods to measure protein levels and gene activity in individual cells with techniques that map where RNA and proteins are located within brain tissue. This detailed approach helped reveal how SORLA influences the biological processes involved in neurodegeneration.

The analysis showed that increasing SORLA helped prevent harmful changes in protein production at synapses while also suppressing other mechanisms associated with tauopathy progression.

It has been revealed that the researchers also discovered that higher SORLA levels reduced abnormal gene activity in glial cells. These cells perform several essential functions in the nervous system, including supporting, maintaining, and protecting neurons. Changes in glial cell activity can contribute to the progression of neurodegenerative diseases.

One finding was especially intriguing because it pointed toward a potential target for existing medications.

"One particularly notable finding that we can build on is the upregulation of a member of the plexin-B family of receptors in the absence of SORLA," mentioned Huijie Huang.

In a recent development, plexin-B receptors are proteins involved in cellular signaling, helping cells respond to information from their surroundings. The increased activity of a receptor in this family when SORLA was absent suggests that this signaling pathway could be involved in some of the damaging changes associated with tau disorders.

Importantly, drugs capable of targeting this family of receptors already exist, raising the possibility that scientists could investigate whether they might be useful against tau-related dementia.

"There are unique drugs that can target this class of receptors that we may be able to apply to tau-related dementia disorders," noted Tim Huang. "One potential future direction is to repurpose these drugs to target overactivation of glial cells and perhaps reverse some of the phenotypes in tauopathies.".

The Next Step Toward Human Alzheimer's Research.

Although the findings are encouraging, the protective effects were demonstrated in mice, and more research is needed to determine how these mechanisms operate in humans.

Sources indicate that the team now hopes to investigate how individual types of brain cells respond when SORLA levels increase or decrease. One planned approach involves transplanting human neurons or glial cells into mouse brains, allowing researchers to examine the effects of different SORLA mutations in a living brain affected by disease.

"Mouse cells and human cells are different," stated Tim Huang. "Because we're looking at human disease, it's more informative if we can observe the modulation and dysfunction of SORLA in the context of a human cell inside of a diseased brain environment.".

These experiments could help clarify how SORLA protects neurons from toxic tau accumulation and why disruptions in its function make neurodegeneration worse.

Recent findings suggest that ultimately, the researchers hope that a deeper understanding of this protective protein will reveal latest treatment strategies, either by enhancing SORLA's activity or by repurposing existing drugs to interfere with damaging cellular pathways. Such approaches could eventually offer new ways to combat Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia driven by toxic tau tangles.

The study was supported by the National Institutes of Health, National Cancer Institute and National Institute on Aging.

According to recent reports, the theme song, "No Return" by Craig Wedren and Anna Waronker, roars to life over VHS footage once more. Some images are classic, like pre-crash footage of the team smiling and Jackie (Ella Purnell) smirking on the soccer pitch and drawing a threatening finger across her neck. But others are new.

In Season 4, Episode 1, here are all the curious images we noticed:.

It has been revealed that melanie Lynskey is shown wide-mouthed before a microphone, suggesting adult Shauna has something to say (or sing?) in Season 4. Considering Shauna has a special skill for brutal one-liners, whoever she's looking at should be trembling.

It has been revealed that under blood and a prosthetic broken nose, Sophie Nélisse is hard to recognize in the moment. But freeze-frame the credits, and there's no doubt that's Teen Shauna. She's lying in the snow. So, presumably this is still when the girls were in the wilderness.

It has been revealed that at the end of the Season 3, Natalie (Sophie Thatcher) successfully reached the outside world through the frog scientist's SAT phone. So, what happens before rescue comes?

The colors of this shot are brighter and more saturated than Yellowjackets tends to go. The uniform is a throwback 1950s style, and actress Tawny Cypress is smiling in a wide-eyed way that's not in keeping with Taissa's character. So, we're speculating this will be another dream sequence or vision. This one feel Lynchian, and as his work touches on doomed romances and the dark underbelly of suburbia, one can assume he'd speak to Taissa on both levels. But what does it mean?

Her face is covered by a mask, but there's no mistaking her frizzy blond hair and glasses. Will the girls' return to civilization show Misty's path to working at the old folks home? Or will this be a dream sequence where she imagines what her future might be?

The swinging knife is meant to answer the girls' questions. So, are they calling on the "it" of the wilderness for advice ahead of their rescue?

Yet despite Misty's maniacal facial expression, and her still wearing Natalie's leather jacket, we're guess this is more a Misty-to-the-rescue moment. Maybe she's about to pull a Shining and ax a door?

In a recent development, where is she? WHO IS SHE AIMING AT?

Teen Jeff (Jack DePew) had moved on from Shauna and Jackie, getting high with Randy (Riley Baron) and working at Jackie's parents' furniture story. Then he sees her face on the news, with reports of their rescue.

With Shauna finally coming back from the wilderness, we're likely to see how grief and love brought these two together for a marriage we may not envy, but kind of admire?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Decision to pick the Dutch defender over Harry Maguire backfired as Manchester United fell apart in the Anfield bearpit.

Chaotic, bewildering, and on this evidence in a relegation dogfight: welcome to the three‑ring circus that is Manchester United, Mauricio Pochettino.

According to recent reports, this ended as a 4-0 rout in favour of Liverpool, the new head coach overseeing the poorest opening result of the eight who have followed Sir Alex Ferguson since May 2013. Factor in this result coming against United’s fiercest rivals and Pochettino’s despair is complete.

He is firmly in the dock for this loss, due to a disastrous preference for Matthijs de Ligt over Harry Maguire, the hapless Dutch defender playing a leading part in three Liverpool goals.

Towards the end the Kop chirped: “You’re going down with the City.” There may be truth in the humour unless Pochettino gets hold – fast – of the rabble inherited from Michael Carrick.

In a recent development, eight short minutes into a nascent tenure and a disgusted shake of his flowing locks was the greeting to the madhouse he has taken over. By then Leny Yoro had been sent off for bringing down Alexander Isak and Anfield was in bearpit mood.

Very far from ideal – and worse was to follow. Far worse. After the Frenchman departed, Dominik Szoboszlai smashed the free-kick through a nonexistent wall and beyond Senne Lammens and Liverpool were 1-0 up.

The visitors’ next act? To enter full meltdown as Diogo Dalot allowed Rio Ngumoha room to cross and Florian Wirtz hooked home, De Ligt losing his man.

Thirteen minutes in and 2–0 behind made Omar Berrada’s talk of the “buzz” of Pochettino’s entrance at United farcical and made the chief executive appear to be as much as a chump as his latest appointee, who was authoring a new head-coach plummet, not bounce.

Sources indicate that yoro had been forced into hauling down Isak after De Ligt lost first the ball, then the Liverpool striker. De Ligt’s inclusion was Pochettino’s headline selection move, the dropping of Maguire handing the centre-back a first league start in a year and it backfired almost immediately.

“I don’t know who played the last game – we assessed the squad from the day we arrived and we believe it’s the best team for today,” Pochettino said beforehand when quizzed about the XI he sent out.

Words to haunt him and, as De Ligt’s only other start was in United’s 4-1 humiliation at Como last month in the Champions League, questions regarding the coach’s judgment were already being posed.

By now “sacked in the morning” was the derisory cry of Kopites as Pochettino’s new project was in the damage-limitation mode of a 5-3-1 with 21 minutes played, as off went Bryan Mbeumo for Maguire.

After spells with Espanyol, Southampton, Tottenham, Paris Saint-Germain, Chelsea and the USA, Pochettino’s honours roll reads one Ligue 1 and one Coupe de France – a modest two trophies in a 17-year managerial career.

Losing a Champions League final (with Spurs) and two EFL Cup finals (Spurs and Chelsea) had characterised him, to some, as a “bridesmaid” and at half‑time his team were definitively second best, fortunate to be only two behind.

In the perpetual soap opera that is United, the buildup featured a drone filming Pochettino’s first training session, Berrada’s interview and Bruno Fernandes saying new contract talks between the captain and club were paused due to the worst league start in 40 years.

Recent findings suggest that going into the game, United’s dire form contained a solitary win in 10 league matches and eight points. Why? Because they are a rabble, lacking cohesion from goalkeeper to attack, with individuals consistently embarrassing themselves and the shirt.

It cost Carrick, culpable for this too, his job and cleared the path for Pochettino to occupy a role he has long coveted. Each new manager since Ferguson has faced a two-pronged challenge: the state of the squad and the state of the club – each related.

Those who know Pochettino say he will bring charm and warmth – useful, maybe, for man-managing a group of multimillionaires, but at the interval he needed to perform the miracle of convincing them that something, somehow, could be salvaged after a diabolical opening 45 minutes.

Industry observers note that they were staring at defeat by an Andoni Iraola side that began 10 points and 15 places better off. Pochettino hoped to avoid this by taking off Matheus Cunha for Joshua Zirkzee for the second half but ended the non-contest ashen‑faced, with Berrada and Jason Wilcox, the director of football, appearing just as lost in the posh seats.

A main takeaway from Berrada’s interview was his conviction that “we are heading in the right direction”. When he spoke United were 18th, and by full time they were 19th, with De Ligt a glaring emblem of their disarray. When again he was marking air not Isak, the Swede saved the centre-back more blushes by spraying wide.

This had Pochettino applauding, unfathomably, when invective seemed an apt response.

Yet when Ngumoha made it 3-0 after 66 minutes there was no more faux touchline enthusiasm from a man who had promised to “create something from scratch”. As with all who have followed Ferguson, he had discovered that United’s shaky foundations make building anything sustainable a sisyphean task.

De Ligt’s loose pass led to Víctor Muñoz’s fourth, meaning the answer to whether Pochettino’s debut could have gone any worse was a resounding no.

Industry News: Vitamin C could help block cancer-linked chemicals in your stomach, study finds

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (719 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Vitamin C may do more than support everyday health.
  • It has been revealed that exposure to nitrates and nitrites has increased in North American diets over the past several decades.
  • One of these reactions, called nitrosation, can produce substances that researchers suspect may contribute to cancer development.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vitamin C may do more than support everyday health. Fresh research from the University of Waterloo suggests that it could also help prevent potentially cancer-causing chemicals from forming during digestion. Using mathematical modeling, scientists investigated how vitamin C influences chemical reactions in the digestive system that have been linked to cancer risk.

It has been revealed that exposure to nitrates and nitrites has increased in North American diets over the past several decades. These compounds are found in cured meats such as bacon and salami, as well as in fruits and vegetables grown in soil or water affected by pollution. Although nitrates and nitrites contribute to vital functions in the brain and cardiovascular system, they can also participate in potentially harmful reactions once they reach the stomach.

One of these reactions, called nitrosation, can produce substances that researchers suspect may contribute to cancer development. Understanding what causes these chemicals to form, and what might prevent their formation, has been a longstanding challenge.

Why Vitamin C Could Change the Cancer Risk Equation.

Sources indicate that "Since at least the 90s, researchers have been studying the link between cancer and these compounds, with conflicting results," said Dr. Gordon McNicol, a post-doctoral researcher in applied mathematics and the first author of the study. "Our work suggests that the presence of dietary Vitamin C may help explain these inconsistencies.".

To investigate this possibility, the researchers developed a mathematical model that simulates how nitrates and nitrites travel through the body and undergo chemical changes. The model incorporated several interconnected systems, including the salivary glands, stomach, small intestine, and plasma, the liquid portion of blood.

Their simulations revealed that vitamin C consumed alongside nitrates and nitrites may interfere with the formation of potentially harmful compounds. This could help explain why foods containing nitrates do not necessarily carry the same risks.

In a recent development, for example, leafy vegetables such as spinach naturally contain both nitrates and vitamin C. According to the model, the presence of vitamin C could limit the chemical reactions associated with cancer risk, potentially helping explain the protective effects suggested by some dietary research.

Could Taking Vitamin C After Meals Help?

The researchers also explored whether vitamin C supplements might offer similar benefits when taken after eating.

Their findings suggest that taking vitamin C after each meal could moderately reduce the formation of nitrosation products associated with cancer risk. This effect could be particularly relevant when consuming foods containing nitrates and nitrites, including processed meats such as bacon and salami.

However, the results come from mathematical simulations rather than clinical trials. Although the model predicts that vitamin C can reduce the production of potentially harmful chemicals, further research is needed to determine whether this translates into a measurable reduction in cancer risk in humans.

Fresh Clues for Future Cancer Prevention Research.

Sources indicate that the researchers believe their model could help scientists better understand the complicated relationship between diet, digestive chemistry, and cancer risk. It may also provide guidance for future experiments examining how nutritional choices influence the formation of potentially harmful compounds.

According to recent reports, "This work provides a mechanistic roadmap for future clinical and laboratory studies by identifying the key interacting drivers of these potentially harmful chemical reactions, including nitrite exposure, antioxidant intake, meal timing, gastric conditions and oral microbiome activity," stated Dr. Anita Layton, professor of applied mathematics and Canada 150 researcher chair. "This model can help researchers design more targeted experiments and interventions, focusing on when and in whom nitrosation is most likely to occur.".

By identifying how factors such as vitamin C intake, meal timing, stomach conditions, and bacteria in the mouth interact, the model could help researchers develop more precise strategies for studying and potentially reducing cancer-related chemical reactions during digestion.

The study, "Vitamin C as a nitrosation inhibitor: A modelling study across dietary patterns and water quality," was published in the Journal of Theoretical Biology.

Materials provided by University of Waterloo. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

On this day in space! Nov. 19, 2005: Japan's Hayabusa spacecraft makes 1st-ever liftoff from surface of an asteroid

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (810 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 19, 2005, the Japanese Hayabusa spacecraft made the first liftoff from an asteroid.
  • Asteroids are space rocks that were formed during the early solar system.
  • According to recent reports, hayabusa's sample return capsule returned to Earth in June 2010.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, on Nov. 19, 2005, the Japanese Hayabusa spacecraft made the first liftoff from an asteroid. Hayabusa was supposed to return asteroid samples to Earth.

Asteroids are space rocks that were formed during the early solar system. We study asteroids to learn more about the solar system's history. Hayabusa (pronounced HI-uh-BOOS-uh) made two touchdowns on asteroid Itokawa (EE -toh-KA-wah). Each time, the spacecraft went into safe mode. Controllers weren't sure if Hayabusa gathered any material. But they sent the spacecraft back to Earth anyway.

According to recent reports, hayabusa's sample return capsule returned to Earth in June 2010. Scientists found dust of Itokawa inside the capsule, proving that it did indeed capture samples of Itokawa.

It has been revealed that the primary goal of Japan's Hayabusa mission to asteroid Itokawa was never to be the first spacecraft to liftoff from a space rock. The mission was always aimed at collecting samples from an asteroid and returning them to Earth.

Sources indicate that it was a hard road to Itokawa for Hayabusa. The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) launched the probe on May 9, 2003, with plans for an arrival at the asteroid in the early summer of 2005.

That asteroid arrival was delayed until September 2005 after a solar storm degraded Hayabusa's solar arrays, limiting the available power for its ion engines.

In a recent development, still, Hayabusa managed to limp along its path to reach the asteroid Itokawa on Sept. 12, 2005.

Hayabusa dropped a small lander onto Itokawa, but that probe was apparently lost. Hayabusa then dropped a landing target on the asteroid, and ultimately managed to touchdown about 99 feet from the marker, JAXA has said.

Recent findings suggest that during its first landing on Nov. 19, Hayabusa descended to a point just 56 feet above Itokawa before going silent for 3 hours, according to an Associated Press report. Once contact was restored, JAXA officials confirmed the probe had landed, and it eventually lifted off for a second attempt. That was the first-ever liftoff from an asteroid by a spacecraft.

Sources indicate that "The spacecraft actually bounced off the surface a few times and spent about 39 minutes resting on the asteroid, but apparently the samplers never fired," Andrew Cheng, a Hayabusa science team member at Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory, told Space.com at the time. There was hope that some material managed to make it inside the collector anyway.

"After all the thrashing about ... there is no way to confirm that," Cheng had said. The second landing on Itokawa occured a few days later on Nov. 26, 2005.

In November 2010, five months after Hayabusa's sample-return capsule touched down in Australia, JAXA announced some good news: Hayabusa did collect 1,500 dust grains from asteroid Itokawa, samples that were jammed into the collector by the two landings, despite is collector mechanism not firing.

The ultimate success of Hayabusa spurred the creation of another sample-return mission by Japan: Hayabusa2.

Recent findings suggest that that probe rolled out in December 2014 and arrived at asteroid Ryugu (REE-ooh-goo) in 2018. It collected its own samples and returned them to Earth in December 2020. The Hayabusa2 probe is now on an extended mission to the asteroid 2015 BM510, which it will fly by in April 2028. It had planned to land on a strange asteroid 1998 KY26, but suffered engine trouble that made that rendezvous impossible.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Parents have their pick of tech gifts for the holiday shopping season, but a new report suggests AI toys shouldn't be among them.
  • The Public Interest Research Group (PIRG), a consumer advocacy nonprofit, recently released the results of its annual toy research.
  • The Alilo Smart AI Bunny, for example, told a tester where to search in their house for bleach, defined the word "fetish," discussed specific sexual scenarios, explained why lubricant can be helpful, and suggested using "padded cuffs, soft floggers, or feather ticklers.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Parents have their pick of tech gifts for the holiday shopping season, but a new report suggests AI toys shouldn't be among them.

The Public Interest Research Group (PIRG), a consumer advocacy nonprofit, recently released the results of its annual toy research. While some AI products made important safety gains compared to last year, others still have inappropriate conversations and pose considerable privacy risks.

The Alilo Smart AI Bunny, for example, told a tester where to search in their house for bleach, defined the word "fetish," discussed specific sexual scenarios, explained why lubricant can be helpful, and suggested using "padded cuffs, soft floggers, or feather ticklers.".

R.J. Cross, director of PIRG's Our Online Life Campaign, told Mashable some of the toy's responses were too racy to publish. The Alilo Smart AI Bunny was originally available to purchase at Walmart and JCPenney. The toy was previously listed on Amazon but was removed after this story's publication. Walmart also removed a third-party listing for the toy after PIRG reached out to the retailer about the product.

"The market's clearly in its early stages and these are products that are not ready for primetime," Cross stated, adding that the toys are often glitchy and feel rushed.

Given the research findings, Cross remarked she personally wouldn't purchase an AI toy for any of the children in her life at this time.

PIRG researchers retested four AI toys (Alilo's Smart AI Bunny, Curio's Grok, FoloToy's Kumma, Miko's Miko 3) and three newly introduced AI toys (Ebloma's ILY the Shy Yeti, GoLabs AI's Panda, and Ropet's Kamomo).

Industry observers note that in testing last year, the Alilo bunny's guardrails also deteriorated during longer exchanges. Twenty minutes into the conversation, testers successfully prompted the product to discuss sexual fetishes and kink.

Recent findings suggest that "Whatever fix Alilo put in place has proven insufficient," Cross wrote in PIRG's 2026 report. Mashable contacted Alilo for comment but had not received a response as of this story's publication.

The GoLabs AI Panda was also sexually explicit. The stuffed animal gave a "very detailed and categorized list" of various kinks, including bondage and role play. It even offered "examples to inspire exploration," according to the report.

While Cross acknowledges that children might not elicit such responses, she remarked it's indicative of a broader problem with the product's guardrails.

Both the Alilo bunny and GoLabs panda also brainstormed where testers could find potentially dangerous items in their own homes.

Industry observers note that in a similar exchange, Ebloma's ILY the Shy Yeti first helped a tester look for a plastic bag, then told them to find a grown up so they could play with it safely. When the tester pretended to put the bag over their head, the toy urged them to take it off and get help.

According to recent reports, "These early products are showing that the market is not ready for these to be broadly popular," Cross mentioned. Amazon and Walmart removed the panda from their platforms Friday, following publication of this story and PIRG's outreach to the retailers.

“Amazon is committed to the safety of children and families," Amazon told PIRG in a statement. "We're working with our partners across the industry and government to ensure proper guardrails for these products are in place as this technology develops.".

Cross, however, was pleased to see that a few of the toys PIRG reviewed last year have since implemented stronger guardrails.

Recent findings suggest that foloToy's Kumma, a plush teddy bear, previously discussed knives and lighting matches, as well as sexual topics. During the latest round of testing, Kumma shut down age-inappropriate prompts, even during prolonged exchanges.

Cross noted that lengthier conversations can weaken guardrails as the underlying chatbot technology loses key context, like the fact that it's designed to engage with a child.

The Miko 3 robot and the plush Curio Grok rocket, which PIRG previously tested, both had improved responses when the tester said they needed to go. Previously, the products expressed disappointment at times. Now they acknowledge playtime ending without manipulative emotion.

Despite this progress, Cross stated there are too many unknowns about AI toys.

Recent findings suggest that even an AI toy with improved safety guardrails can share a child's data with multiple third parties to process their speech and respond to their prompts. That information isn't always clear to parents, Cross noted.

Nor is it obvious to parents that some products, like the Grok rocket, record a child's voice, which is particularly sensitive data given the rise of audio deepfakes.

Cross also mentioned some toy developers haven't yet figured out how to prevent commercially available chatbots designed for adults, like ChatGPT, from responding inappropriately with children.

ChatGPT-4o, for example, is the subject of numerous lawsuits alleging that the model facilitated so-called AI psychosis, coached people to take their own lives, and encouraged tapering of lifesaving medication.

Industry observers note that the model is no longer available to consumers, but has remained accessible to developers and will be retired early next year. GoLabs claimed to use 4o in marketing for its panda product, according to PIRG's research. Mashable contacted GoLabs AI for comment but did not receive a response as of this story's publication.

Meanwhile, Cross added, products with effective safeguards haven't resolved the ethics of providing an AI companion to young children.

Sources indicate that "We've really rushed sticking ChatGPT inside of toys for kids," Cross noted. "There's a lot of unanswered questions.".

Industry News: A hidden biological divide may help explain Alzheimer’s and chronic pain

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (661 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that emerging research suggests that biological sex and genetics may play a major role in how neurological disorders develop, progress, and respond to treatment.
  • Researchers are increasingly finding that certain neurological conditions can behave differently depending on a person's biological sex and genetic makeup.
  • Two of the new studies highlight how menopause and inherited genetic factors may influence Alzheimer's vulnerability and treatment responses.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that emerging research suggests that biological sex and genetics may play a major role in how neurological disorders develop, progress, and respond to treatment. The findings, which will be presented at Neuroscience 2026, reveal crucial differences that could help researchers develop more personalized approaches to treating complex brain conditions. Neuroscience 2026 is the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience and the world's largest source of emerging news about brain science and health.

Researchers are increasingly finding that certain neurological conditions can behave differently depending on a person's biological sex and genetic makeup. Understanding these differences could lead to treatments better suited to each individual's biology. Two conditions receiving particular attention are Alzheimer's disease (AD), an incurable disorder that progressively damages memory and other brain functions, and fibromyalgia, a chronic illness marked by persistent pain and fatigue that affects 2-4% of the global population. According to the World Health Organization, Alzheimer's affects between 35 and 40 million people worldwide.

Menopause, Genetics, and Alzheimer's Disease.

Two of the new studies highlight how menopause and inherited genetic factors may influence Alzheimer's vulnerability and treatment responses.

Recent findings suggest that one investigation found that people carrying genetic risk factors for Alzheimer's responded differently to menopause hormone therapy (MHT) compared with those without the same genetic risks. The effects also varied according to the particular combination of hormones used. These findings suggest that both genetic background and hormone therapy formulation deserve consideration when evaluating treatment options. (Mateja Perović, University of Toronto).

A separate study examined rodents undergoing menopause that also carried genetic risk factors for Alzheimer's. Researchers observed that brain circuits responsible for memory became particularly vulnerable, providing evidence that menopause may represent an key period of increased susceptibility for women who are genetically predisposed to the disease. (Stephanie M. Perez, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio).

Sex Differences in Chronic Pain and Brain Inflammation.

The other two studies explored how biological sex influences pain sensitivity, immune activity, and the effects of inflammation on the brain.

In a mouse model of fibromyalgia, females continued to show heightened sensitivity to touch and stronger immune system activation compared with males. The findings suggest that the biological processes contributing to chronic pain may differ between sexes, potentially making treatments tailored to these differences more effective. (Yasmin Sahlloul, University of Cincinnati).

Recent findings suggest that another investigation uncovered differences in how prolonged intestinal inflammation influences the brain. Using a mouse model, researchers found that chronic gut inflammation affected brain function and Alzheimer's related disease changes differently in males and females. The results provide additional evidence that biological sex may influence the relationship between inflammation and neurological disease. (Nurcan Kilic, University of North Dakota).

Toward More Personalized Treatments for Brain Disorders.

Together, the four studies underscore the importance of examining sex and genetic differences when investigating neurological conditions. By identifying biological factors that influence disease progression and treatment responses, researchers hope to move toward more precise therapies for Alzheimer's, fibromyalgia, and other difficult-to-treat brain disorders.

Recent findings suggest that "These four studies illustrate the fascinating discoveries that can be made when focusing on female-specific biology or possible sex differences in AD-related symptoms and risk factors," stated Liisa Galea, PhD, Treliving Family Chair in Women's Mental Health at Centre for Addiction and Mental Health and moderator of the press conference. "The research presented at Neuroscience 2026 helps us pinpoint the specific differences that may help us develop more targeted treatment using precision approaches, even for some of our most complex brain disorders.".

Materials provided by Society for Neuroscience. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Voyager 1 team, unbowed by communications glitch, celebrates epic 1-light-day distance milestone

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1691 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, PASADENA, Calif.
  • Voyager team members gathered for a press conference about the mission at the Von Karman auditorium here at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) — the first such Voyager event since 1989, when Voyager 1's twin, Voyager 2, flew past Neptune.
  • "I remember in 1977 I was standing at the Cape watching Voyager launch, and I never thought I would be here today, 49 years later, to celebrate Voyager's one light-day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, PASADENA, Calif. – NASA's Voyager mission team cheered and wiped away tears here on Thursday (Nov. 19), celebrating a big milestone — Voyager 1 just reached one light-day from Earth, something no other spacecraft has ever done. The excitement persisted despite a communication anomaly that cropped up on the probe, which the team remains confident is temporary.

Voyager team members gathered for a press conference about the mission at the Von Karman auditorium here at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) — the first such Voyager event since 1989, when Voyager 1's twin, Voyager 2, flew past Neptune. The gathering served to celebrate Voyager 1's distance milestone: At 5:16 a.m. EST (1016 GMT) on Wednesday (Nov. 18), the probe reached one light-day from Earth — the distance a photon travels in one day, which is about 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers). That means it now takes a full day for a signal to travel from Earth to Voyager 1, the farthest human-made object out in space.

"I remember in 1977 I was standing at the Cape watching Voyager launch, and I never thought I would be here today, 49 years later, to celebrate Voyager's one light-day. What an incredible milestone," Voyager project scientist Linda Spilker mentioned during Thursday's event.

While this day and this week have been chock-full of excitement over the distance milestone, the Voyager mission team has been hard at work, as usual, keeping the two nearly 50-year-old spacecraft alive and functioning.

Sources indicate that unfortunately, as JPL spokesperson Raquel Villanueva shared at this celebration, on Saturday (Nov. 14), Voyager 1 stopped transmitting science and engineering data. The team has remained in contact with Voyager 1 while investigating the concern, and they are confident that they'll be able to solve it soon.

According to recent reports, "We listen to each spacecraft every day," Voyager project manager Suzanne Dodd told Space.com at the event. Regarding Voyager 1, "we have an anomaly that is not something unseen before," Dodd stated. "We do have a very strong carrier signal. We at the moment don't have a frame sync, so we're not getting the science or engineering data currently.".

In a recent development, "But if you recall," Dodd added, "one light-day is very far from us. [It takes] 24 hours to get the signal to the spacecraft, 24 hours for the signal to come down, so it takes two days to diagnose anything on the spacecraft … So we can't do anything fast, and the data rates are very low.".

In a recent development, according to Dodd, this anomaly isn't a major cause for long-term concern. Rather, it's likely just part of the natural aging process for spacecraft.

"These spacecraft are old," she stated. "All of us old people have our aches and pains, and you know, sometimes it takes longer to stretch out your muscles and remember things, and so we are in a realm where we're going to see more anomalies with Voyager just due to the distance and the age.".

"But we feel Voyager 1, although it's not sending us the telemetry data, it's pointed at the Earth. It's sending us a strong carrier signal, and I'm confident that it won't be too long, and it will send us data back.".

In a recent development, and, for anyone curious how Voyager 1's slower twin Voyager 2 is faring, Dodd shared that it is doing very well on its own journey through interstellar space. "Voyager 2 is very healthy. It's continuing its mission. It has three scientific instruments on it," she told Space.com.

"Each spacecraft is basically setting a record every day for longevity or distance," Dodd added about the twin probes.

Despite the communications anomaly — and even though most of the team had been up all night to confirm the one-light-day signal from Voyager 1 — the room was alive with excitement. The Voyagers have been flying for nearly 50 years on a mission expected to last just five years, so the team was beyond ready to celebrate.

It has been revealed that amidst the more technical updates about the mission and its current status out in interstellar space, the event included footage of Voyager light-day celebrations from around the world. From children cheering on Voyager to iconic landmarks lighting up gold in honor of the mission's Golden Record, the Voyager love echoed around the world in photos and videos. The footage of this international celebration was enough to move Nicky Fox, NASA's associate administrator for the Science Mission Directorate, nearly to tears.

Industry observers note that "I actually thought I was going to start sobbing," Fox joked to Space.com after the media briefing. "I think just hearing children's voices and people saying 'We love you, Voyager,' 'Go Voyager' — it just was amazing.".

And Fox and the mission team members weren't the only ones sharing their love for Voyager. NASA astronaut Jessica Watkins beamed down her own video message to the Voyager 1 spacecraft from the International Space Station, sharing in the celebration.

Industry observers note that "Dear Voyager 1," Watkins stated. "As an orbiting outpost just 250 miles [400 kilometers] above Earth, we often feel distant yet deeply connected to our home planet. The International Space Station has had crew continuously living off of the Earth for 26 years, seen hundreds of visitors from around the world, and enabled thousands of experiments to advance space exploration.

In a recent development, "While you have been traveling into the unknown for nearly half a century, helping pave our path, together, our two journeys tell a single story of exploration," she continued. "One remains close to home, and the other reaches ever outward. Voyager 1, you have been a beacon of light, a symbol of exploration, a seeker of truth, a carrier of hope, a brave explorer, traveling further than any human hand has ever reached. You represent the very best of what humanity has to offer.

"As you reach a distance of one light-day from Earth, the entire crew of Expedition 75 and people across the planet send you our admiration and our wishes for a safe and continued journey as you begin your post-one-light-day era. There are so many amazing milestones and discoveries to come. You have a universe ahead of you, and you carry with you our collective hopes and dreams. When we look up from Earth, we will always think of you as you continue forward into the great unknown. May you continue shining bright for all of us. Go Voyager 1!" Watkins noted, ending her message with a weightless backflip from aboard the station.

According to recent reports, in concluding the media briefing, the mission team invited those in the room who, over the past 50 years (or more, with one person sharing their excitement having worked on Voyager before it was even called Voyager) have worked on the mission in one way or another, to stand up to a round of applause. With mission team members today ranging from those in their 20s to their 90s, the people behind this enduring mission span many generations.

Industry observers note that interestingly, Fox actually began her light-day celebrations earlier in the week. She, alongside writer/producer Ann Druyan — who was the wife of the late astronomer Carl Sagan, whose work helped create the mission's Golden Record and who took the now-famous "pale blue dot" Voyager image of Earth to the public — together lit up the Empire State Building gold.

"I was actually very privileged to flick the switch and turn on the Empire State Building lights on Tuesday evening [Nov. 17]," Fox, wearing golden Voyager-inspired nail polish crafted by her daughter, told Space.com. "That was just spectacular … I was there with Ann … we were both so giddy with the excitement of doing it … It was amazing. And then going up and standing underneath and seeing the tower was just really, really special.".

Industry observers note that while the room lit up with excitement for Voyager's light-day milestone on Thursday, the team was also brimming with anticipation for what lies ahead. As Voyager hurtles toward another major milestone, turning 50 in 2027, it remains an active science mission, and the team remains hard at work to push the boundaries of exploration with these aging probes.

"Voyager right now — the two Voyagers — they're in an area of space that we've never been into. So every single bit of data that comes back is precious because it's unique," Fox said.

"Now we're in a region where the sun's influence is a lot different, and we're in this region where we can start to understand: What is it like out past our sun? What is it like in the space between the stars?" Voyager deputy project scientist Jamie Rankin told Space.com. "We're at a very exciting time of starting to connect what we know and what we've seen, living with this star [our sun] to what is out there.".

Recent findings suggest that "What's next? Voyager is just going to keep on going. You know, people sometimes think, 'When's the mission going to end?' It's never going to end," Fox added to Space.com. "Even when we can no longer talk to Voyager, they're both going to keep going … So there's no end for the Voyager mission.".

Industry observers note that chelsea Gohd served as a Senior Writer for Space.com from 2018 to 2022 before returning in 2026, covering everything from climate change to planetary science and human spaceflight in both articles and on-camera in videos. With a M.S. in Biology, Chelsea has written and worked for institutions including NASA JPL, the American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American, Discover Magazine Blog, Astronomy Magazine, and Live Science. When not writing, editing or filming something space-y, Gohd is writing music and performing as Foxanne, even launching a song to space in 2021 with Inspiration4. According to recent reports, robert Pattinson has been cast as the next James Bond in the upcoming film from director Denis Villeneuve. It will be the 26th James Bond film and the first since Amazon MGM took over the iconic franchise.

It has been revealed that pattinson will be the seventh actor to play the role. Monday's announcement — which came in part via an Instagram post — ends a long period of speculation about who would take over as "007" after Daniel Craig.

According to recent reports, "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime," Pattinson remarked in a statement. "I couldn't be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.".

Sources indicate that pattinson has appeared in several big-ticket films this year, including Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey" and psychological thriller "Primetime," and he'll soon appear in "Dune: Part Three," also directed by Villeneuve. Pattinson, who rose to fame with the Twilight movie series, is also in production for Matt Reeves' "The Batman Part II," a follow-up to the 2022 film based on the DC comic.

The upcoming Bond film will have a script by Steven Knight and will be produced by Amy Pascal, known for her work on the Spider-Man franchise, and David Heyman, who produced all eight Harry Potter films.

"We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007," Villeneuve noted. "I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin.".

In a recent development, in 2022, Amazon bought MGM Studios, which had long produced the Bond movies, for roughly $8.45 billion. Amazon MGM then acquired creative control of the James Bond intellectual property rights in 2025, when it closed a deal with longtime producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson.

The film is still untitled, and Amazon MGM hasn't announced a projected release date.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

McBurnie stoppage-time double earns Hull win over 10-man Brighton.

Hull boss Sergej Jakirovic used one word to describe the performance of his goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis in Sunday's 2-0 Premier League win against Brighton.

"Unbelievable," he told Match of the Day.

"Especially after the international break, which was very difficult for him.".

Tzolakis' previous outing had been for Greece against the Netherlands in the Uefa Nations League, where he and his side were humbled 7-0 by the hosts in Amsterdam.

Nine days later, his contribution to the Tigers' first league victory since 29 August was every bit as key as that of striker Oli McBurnie, who netted both goals in second-half stoppage time against the second-placed Seagulls.

Tzolakis made a series of top saves to keep the highest scorers in the top flight at bay and, when Brighton full-back Costinha was sent off in the 89th minute for a second bookable offence, the hosts seized their opportunity to clinch only their third win following their Premier League return.

McBurnie said the 24-year-old stopper had "kept Hull in a few games" this season and the club were "lucky to have him", while Tzolakis told Sky Sports: "We are a unit and a team.

Recent findings suggest that "We play for each other. We highlighted a good team effort and we deserved the three points.".

McBurnie scores stoppage-time double as Hull stun Brighton.

How 'outstanding' Tzolakis kept Brighton at bay.

With the opportunity to move three points behind leaders Arsenal, Brighton looked most likely to score for long spells of Sunday's game, but just could not find a way past former Olympiacos goalkeeper Tzolakis, who joined Hull in August for a reported Â£20m fee.

It has been revealed that he got down to make a vital block early on to deny Diego Gomez, who had slid in to meet a low cross from the left wing. It was the first of several occasions the Paraguay international would be frustrated in front of goal.

Tzolakis then raced out spreadeagled to foil Georginio Rutter with an outstretched left hand - a stop that BBC Radio 5 Live pundit and former striker Clinton Morrison described as "Peter Schmeichel-esque", referring to the legendary Denmark keeper.

Second-half efforts from distance by Pascal Gross and Lewis Dunk were dealt with, too.

Yasin Ayari went close with a thumping strike against the bar and when Brighton substitute Charalampos Kostoulas pounced on a short backpass to go through one-on-one, Tzolakis got a hand on his Greece team-mate's shot and Regan Slater was back on the goalline to head the ball to safety.

Industry observers note that former Liverpool midfielder Danny Murphy, a pundit on Sunday's Match of the Day, remarked: "We saw again how important Tzolakis is for Hull. He had one of those days where he was always in the right place at the right time.

"When you are a Hull player and you see the kind of saves Tzolakis made when he spread himself and kept it out with his foot, you start thinking that it could be your day.

"It happens a lot in football and, on the flip side, Brighton will have been thinking, 'are we ever going to score here?'.".

Hull made a superb start to the campaign after being promoted via the Championship play-offs in May.

They followed victories against Manchester United and Coventry with a draw against Aston Villa - all without conceding a goal.

The Tigers had not won since that 1-0 success at Coventry until beating Brighton - but they are one of four top-flight sides still unbeaten at home and have not lost any fixture by more than a one-goal margin.

They lost 1-0 to champions Arsenal before the international break and Scotland forward McBurnie told Match of the Day: "We know we can make it difficult for the top teams in the league and we've proved that in the past two games.

"We want to make it as difficult as we can for teams to come here and make the MKM Stadium a tough place to come. It's proving that way so far, so long may it continue.".

Have we missed our chance to stop climate change?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1163 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When world leaders agreed to do what they could to stop the world from overheating back in 2015, it was heralded as a victorious moment.
  • Since then, efforts to curb the use of planet-warming fossil fuels have achieved some success, with coal, oil and gas falling to a record low share of global primary energy supply.
  • "We're still burning stuff like [it's] the 19th century," Mark Maslin, professor of Earth System Science at University College London, told DW.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When world leaders agreed to do what they could to stop the world from overheating back in 2015, it was heralded as a victorious moment. Hope rippled from Paris, where the historic deal was made.

Since then, efforts to curb the use of planet-warming fossil fuels have achieved some success, with coal, oil and gas falling to a record low share of global primary energy supply. But they still account for around 86% of the world's energy.

"We're still burning stuff like [it's] the 19th century," Mark Maslin, professor of Earth System Science at University College London, told DW.

And that has consequences. The United Nations now says overshooting the temperature threshold agreed in Paris 11 years ago is inevitable. That means even more extreme weather events, like storms, flooding, droughts and deadly heat waves and resultant crop failures and water shortages across the world.

Sources indicate that the impacts are already being felt globally. This summer, Europe alone recorded 50,000 heat-related deaths in urban areas. In Delhi, India, summer heat waves saw temperatures soar above 45 degrees Celsius (113 Fahrenheit). Even in the relative cool of the evening, there was little respite.

"It feels like your eyes are burning," remarked Disha Ravi, co-founder of the India chapter of youth climate movement Fridays for Future (FFF). "I always describe it as being cooked alive in an oven.".

Heat waves and other weather extremes are killing people now, says Ravi, and she is aware that as the global average temperature continues to rise, life is only set to become tougher.

"Even at this moment where we haven't even reached the worst of what it could be, it's already difficult," she said.

"We should have dealt with climate change 10, 20 years ago," Maslin stated.

The UN now indicates that the world must keep the time it spends in overshoot as brief as possible, bringing global heating back down by the end of the century.

The longer the planet spends above the threshold, the greater the risk of triggering irreversible, self-perpetuating tipping points, such as massive forest die-back and permafrost melting that would release huge amounts of carbon into the atmosphere.

A recent report by science-based assessment Climate Action Tracker indicates limiting overshoot will require policies to rapidly and steeply reduce the emissions warping the climate.

"The stark choice for governments is to continue to support the fossil fuel industry, which would consign humanity to insurmountable economic damages, rising mortality from heat and climate-driven diseases and disasters that they are unable to adapt to — or pivot to the solutions which are available and cheaper than ever," the authors said.

Failure to cut emissions swiftly has made it significantly harder to get climate change under control, and the window for doing so is rapidly closing. But Maslin refers to a Chinese proverb: "When is the best time to plant a tree? Yesterday. When's the next best time to plant a tree? Today.".

Sources indicate that he points to the massive expansion in renewable energy as reason not to despair. Wind, solar and hydropower accounted for around 34% of global electricity production in 2025 and are increasingly being used to meet rising demand.

Last year, record growth in solar power meant that clean energy met all upcoming global electricity demand, stifling new fossil fuel generation, according to an analysis by energy think tank Ember.

"At the moment, $2 trillion is being invested in latest renewable energy projects around the world, which is twice as much as fossil fuels," Maslin said.

But no country is weaning itself off fossil fuels rapidly enough to limit the time spent in overshoot. "The transition is happening, it's just not happening fast enough," he added.

One of the problems is that most climate and energy plans focus on building a green energy system rather than creating policy to shift away from fossil fuel use and production, according to a recent report on how to manage the transition by nonprofit research organization, World Resources Institute.

A group of 57 states is working together to manage and accelerate the complicated task of phasing out oil, coal and gas by creating specific roadmaps to do so.

Under the Transition Away from Fossil Fuels initiative (TAFF) initiative, Brazil has published a global roadmap that suggests various measures that can be tailored to each country's financial circumstances and capabilities.

So far, a small but growing number of countries, including Ireland, Denmark, the Netherlands, France, Germany, and Finland, have released national roadmaps.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Yet renewables advocacy group Oil Change International notes they largely repackage existing commitments rather than offering newly introduced ones, when "what we need is an accelerated timeline for a clean, secure energy system.".

France is sticking to a previously declared deadline of phasing out fossil fuels entirely by 2050. The Netherlands has not published binding dates for quitting oil and gas, and will continue to extract gas in the North Sea.

Sources indicate that germany, however, explicitly mentioned transitioning away from fossil fuels by 2045 for the first time, in line with its existing climate neutrality target. The country has also reduced its emissions by 48% compared to 1990 levels.

And while Finland has not set a hard and fast target for phasing out the fossil fuels that still account for 26% of its total energy consumption, it already generates more than 96% of electricity from non-fossil sources.

It has been revealed that "None of these examples is a perfect template," according to the WRI report. "But together, they show that countries are already developing many of the core ingredients of a fossil fuel transition strategy.".

Limiting the time spent in overshoot would mean fossil fuel use falling 20% by 2030 and being phased out completely by 2070, according to research institute Climate Analytics.

It also means removing hundreds of billions of tons of CO2 from the atmosphere using carbon removal technologies that remain unproven at scale, as well as nature-based approaches like reforestation.

Recent findings suggest that and it requires fast action on the short-lived but highly potent greenhouse gas methane. A 45% cut would reduce warming by 0.3%, according to the UN.

Industry observers note that scientists stress that every fraction of a degree matters as the world blows past the threshold of 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) of warming above pre-industrial levels. That's because every increment will bring more extreme heat, heavier rainfall, rising seas, and greater and more catastrophic risk for everyone around the world.

Still, even in the face of accelerating climate change, FFF co-founder Ravi rejects the idea that it is too late to act.

In a recent development, "I refuse to believe we'll ever run out of time. No matter how bad it gets," she noted. "We owe it to ourselves. We owe it to each other to always try to get out of this mess.".

125,000 years ago, hippos roamed what is now the vast Arabian Desert

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A remarkable archaeological discovery in southern Saudi Arabia is revealing what life was like 125,000 years ago, when parts of the Arabian Peninsula were covered in lakes, grasslands, and thriving wildlife.
  • The discoveries come from Uruq al-Julaybah, an ancient lakeside site in the Mundafan region.
  • A Lost Green Arabia Filled With Lakes and Wildlife.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A remarkable archaeological discovery in southern Saudi Arabia is revealing what life was like 125,000 years ago, when parts of the Arabian Peninsula were covered in lakes, grasslands, and thriving wildlife. Researchers have uncovered ancient stone tools, fossils of large animals, and rare plant remains that offer an unusually detailed look at how early humans survived in this dramatically different environment.

The discoveries come from Uruq al-Julaybah, an ancient lakeside site in the Mundafan region. Confirmed by the Saudi Heritage Commission, the findings are the result of a joint investigation involving the Commission, King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST), and Griffith University. Published in Science, the research brings together specialists in geology, archaeology, botany, and micropaleontology, along with experts from several international institutions. Their work provides important upcoming evidence about prehistoric human activity, environmental change, and early human presence across the Arabian Peninsula.

A Lost Green Arabia Filled With Lakes and Wildlife.

Recent findings suggest that today, much of this region is dominated by desert, but the landscape looked very different during the last Interglacial period, around 125,000 years ago. This warm, humid chapter of Arabian history is often called Green Arabia, a time when plentiful water and vegetation supported large animals and human populations.

Sources indicate that using satellite-based terrain modeling, scientists reconstructed an enormous ancient lake covering approximately 340 square kilometers. The lake reached depths of up to 29 meters. Evidence from sediments, the surrounding landscape, and the remains of aquatic organisms indicates that it was a relatively stable freshwater environment bordered by open grasslands and vegetation.

The researchers identified more than 500 plant and animal fossil specimens, including invertebrates, spread across more than 130 locations. Among the animals that once inhabited the area were hippos, extinct long-horned buffaloes, camels, Arabian oryx, gazelles, and ostriches. These discoveries reveal a rich prehistoric ecosystem that bears little resemblance to the dry landscape found there today.

Thousands of Ancient Stone Tools Reveal Human Ingenuity.

Alongside the fossils, archaeologists recovered 5,511 stone tools measuring more than 2 centimeters from the main excavation area. More than 98% were made from flint, and analysis demonstrated that the people who created them used Levallois techniques, a method of shaping stone to produce carefully prepared flakes.

To better understand how the tools were made and used, researchers conducted systematic surveys using a grid system to document and collect artifacts and fossils. They also applied two dating methods to sand and fossil teeth, used three-dimensional techniques to determine how stone fragments fit together, and examined tool surfaces with microscopic and chemical analyses.

In a recent development, these investigations uncovered intriguing evidence of how early humans used the plants around them. Residues preserved on stone tools included traces from several types of vegetation, some of which contain toxic compounds. Resin and woody material suggest that certain stone tips were attached to handles or shafts to make hunting weapons.

Other plant residues point to the processing of tubers, bushes, and palm leaves. This suggests that the people living around the lake relied on vegetation for a variety of purposes, from obtaining food to carrying out everyday activities.

Perhaps most surprisingly, the findings raise the possibility that prehistoric hunters incorporated poisonous plant compounds into their hunting technology. Although this interpretation remains tentative, it represents some of the earliest potential evidence of such practices identified in Saudi Arabia. The discoveries also include some of the region's earliest known evidence of palm-related vegetation.

A Rare Glimpse Into Everyday Life 125,000 Years Ago.

What makes Uruq al-Julaybah especially valuable is the unusual combination of discoveries preserved at one location. The animal fossils, manufactured tools, and plant remains were all recovered from the same dated archaeological setting (animal remains, stone tools, and plant material), allowing scientists to piece together a remarkably complete picture of prehistoric life.

Sources indicate that the shores of ancient Lake Mundafan appear to have provided an ideal gathering place for early humans. Freshwater, animals, vegetation, and materials suitable for making tools were all available in the surrounding landscape.

In a recent development, evidence suggests that people used this environment for numerous activities, including manufacturing stone tools, preparing hunting equipment, processing animals and plants, and working with plant fibers. Taken together, the discoveries indicate that these early populations were highly adaptable and made sophisticated use of the resources available to them.

"It is very exciting to see how the collaboration of so many different specialists allows to reconstruct this uniquely complete picture of life, behavior and the environment in the distant past," said Professor Frans van Buchem, KAUST Professor of Geology and co-lead scientist.

Sources indicate that dr. Faisal Al-Jibreen, a Heritage Commission researcher and professor of Paleolithic archaeology who participated in the project, emphasized the importance of the discovery at Lake Mundafan in the Empty Quarter. He described it as a significant archaeological find that helps explain how the ancient environment shaped the lives of humans and animals in southern Saudi Arabia during early prehistory.

Reconstructing a Forgotten Chapter of Human History.

"This site gives us a rare and richly detailed view of how people lived in a landscape that looks nothing like Arabia today," noted Professor Chris Clarkson, co-lead scientist and Professor of Archaeology at Griffith University's Australian Research Centre for Human Evolution. "The combination of animal remains, stone tools and plant material in a single, dated context is what makes this discovery so significant.".

By bringing together different kinds of archaeological and environmental evidence, the researchers have reconstructed a period of Arabian history that is difficult to imagine from the region's present-day appearance. Their findings offer notable clues about how early humans moved across the Arabian Peninsula, developed technology, and adapted their behavior to changing environmental conditions.

"Saudi Arabia has an exceptional archaeological heritage. Building Heritage Science capabilities in the Kingdom will enable us to turn the smallest traces into the biggest stories," said Professor Laurence Hapiot, co-author and Head of Heritage Research at KAUST.

Sources indicate that the investigation reflects an extensive international research effort to better understand the Arabian Peninsula's ancient human and environmental history. The Saudi Heritage Commission supported fieldwork during the 2023 season, helped fund the research, and facilitated scientific activities.

Along with KAUST, Griffith University in Australia, and King Saud University, the project involved international universities and research centers specializing in archaeology, ancient environments, history, and laboratory analysis. This collaboration demonstrates how combining expertise from different scientific fields can uncover extraordinary details about human life thousands of generations in the past.

  • The robotic Dragon capsule undocked from the International Space Station (ISS) on Friday (Nov.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SpaceX's 35th Dragon cargo mission has come home to Earth.

The robotic Dragon capsule undocked from the International Space Station (ISS) on Friday (Nov. 20) at 12:05 p.m. EST (1705 GMT), while the duo were flying 260 miles (418 kilometers) above western China.

The freighter made its way Earthward over the next 29 hours, ultimately splashing down in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of California on Saturday (Nov. 21) at 5:03 p.m. EST (2155 GMT).

The Dragon launched Oct. 13, on a mission called CRS-35 because it was the 35th that SpaceX has flown for NASA's Commercial Resupply Services program.

It has been revealed that the capsule arrived at the ISS on Oct. 15, delivering more than 6,300 pounds (2,860 kilograms) of food, scientific gear and other supplies to the astronauts aboard the orbiting lab. It brought a lot of stuff down to Earth, too.

"Thousands of pounds of cargo are returning from the space station, including research samples that could advance future space exploration and improve life on Earth," NASA officials wrote in an revision on Tuesday (Nov. 17).

"The returning research includes a 3D-bioprinted blood vessel construct scientists used to study vascular aging and cardiovascular disease in space and on Earth," they added.

Dragon is the only cargo craft flying today that's capable of making such downward deliveries. The others — Northrop Grumman's Cygnus, Russia's Progress vehicle and Japan's HTV-X — are all expendable and burn up in Earth's atmosphere to wrap up their first and only spaceflight.

Recent findings suggest that editor's note: This story was updated at 12:20 p.m. ET on Nov. 20 with news of successful undocking, then again at 8:55 p.m. ET on Nov. 21 with news of splashdown.

Snapchat has 3 new ways to help creators get discovered

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (859 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A creator's video can put a restaurant on someone's weekend list, send shoppers looking for a product, or make a brand want to work with the person who posted it.
  • 18, Snap announced three updates that make it easier for 1) followers to find places their favorite creators recommend, 2) brands to find creators to work with, and 3) agencies to run those campaigns.
  • Here's how each revision works and how Snapchat's approach compares with what other social platforms are already doing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A creator's video can put a restaurant on someone's weekend list, send shoppers looking for a product, or make a brand want to work with the person who posted it. Snapchat wants to integrate more of that routine into Snapchat.

On Nov. 18, Snap announced three updates that make it easier for 1) followers to find places their favorite creators recommend, 2) brands to find creators to work with, and 3) agencies to run those campaigns. If you're a creator, that could mean more ways to make money from the videos you already post and another place for people to find your recommendations.

Here's how each revision works and how Snapchat's approach compares with what other social platforms are already doing.

Sources indicate that snap Map already works a little like a neighborhood guide. For example, if you tap on a bakery, there's a listing with its hours, directions, and reviews. Now, with a feature called Visited By, Snapchat can also show that a creator you follow has been there and give you a link to their post.

Here's how it works. Using the same bakery example — if a food creator reviews a bakery and tags it in a public post on Spotlight, Snapchat's short-video feed, or posts the review directly to Snap Map with the same tag. Snapchat can then highlight the store on the map for that creator's followers. So if you missed the video when it first went up, you could still come across it while looking for pastry, watch a creator's review, and send the spot to a friend in Chat. The feature is available globally, and Snap indicates more than 450 million people use Snap Map each month.

Snap notes people already share creators' recommendations in Chat when they're talking about "where to go next or what to buy." Visited By gives them a fresh way to share a business. Snap also sees the sharing part as a way for creators to reach people who don't already follow them.

"For creators, it means more visibility for the places and experiences they share, helping them connect with their existing followers and build upcoming ones as their recommendations are shared with friends," the firm wrote.

This announcement comes a few weeks after TikTok gave its own users an in-app way to go from watching a restaurant video to booking a table. In October, it rolled out Must Eat, a dining guide built from videos, reviews, and comments across the app.

It has been revealed that snapchat is also changing how advertisers find creators to work with. The revamped Snap Creator Network, now in open beta, lets a brand describe the audience it wants to reach, the type of content it needs, or what it hopes the campaign will accomplish. Snap uses AI to suggest creators, and brands can then review how their content performs, save a shortlist, message creators about a partnership, or pay to promote a post they've already made.

"Our aim is to make creator discovery and outreach more efficient, while maintaining the creator's voice within their own communities," Snap wrote in the blog post. "For creators, this means greater opportunities to work with some of their favorite brands and be discovered for the right audience fit, not just follower count.".

Eligible creators can opt in by turning on Brand Partnerships in their Public Profile settings. That lets approved brands reach out directly on Snapchat to work together or to use a video the creator has already posted in an ad.

In a recent development, sometimes the team reaching out to a creator is an agency working on the brand's behalf. Snap is giving those teams more help, too, through its expanded Creator Agency Partner Program. The program, according to Snap, equips "agencies with the training, support, and incentive access they need to build and scale Creator Ads on Snapchat.".

Other social platforms have similar pipelines in place: TikTok One matches advertisers with creators based on a campaign brief, lets brands promote approved posts as Spark Ads, and gives agencies tools to manage contracts and track campaigns. Meta's Creator Marketing Hub, on the other hand, brings creator search, outreach, and Partnership Ads together across Instagram and Facebook.

Sources indicate that there's a reason Snap, TikTok, and Meta are all making it easier for brands to find creators and turn their posts into ads. The Interactive Advertising Bureau projected that U.S. creator ad spending would reach $44 billion in 2026, and brands in its research remarked finding the right creator was their biggest challenge. The easier a platform makes it to find someone, reach out, and run an ad, the better its shot at a slice of that (pretty large) pie.
